tagline: See the full picture of data management, governance, and lifecycle—original lessons for visual learners.

modules.title: Why Lifecycle Thinking Matters
modules.summary: Data is not a one-time deliverable. Treating it as a living asset—from first idea to safe disposal—reduces surprises, wasted storage, and trust problems.
keyPoints: A lifecycle shows stages data typically passes through and what good practice looks like at each stage.
Real projects are rarely strictly linear: stages can loop, skip, or run in parallel.
Planning early for retention, access, and deletion is cheaper than fixing chaos later.
Cross-cutting concerns (quality, security, metadata) apply at every stage, not only at the end.
Comparing public models helps you pick language that fits research, enterprise, or mixed contexts.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a data lifecycle?
choices: A fixed vendor product license term
A conceptual map of how data moves from planning through use and end-of-life
quiz.explain: Lifecycle models are teaching and planning tools for stages and responsibilities—not a single software product.

sources.title: Introduction to the Data Lifecycle – UW–Madison

modules.title: Comparing Three Public Lifecycle Models
modules.summary: UW–Madison style training, NIST RDaF, and USGS SDL emphasize similar ideas with different stage names. Learn the overlaps so you can translate across teams.
keyPoints: UW-oriented teaching often highlights Plan, Create, Manage, Use, Share, Collect/Reuse, and Destroy, with continuous management actions.
NIST RDaF organizes research data work into six cyclical stages: Envision, Plan, Generate/Acquire, Process/Analyze, Share/Use/Reuse, Preserve/Discard.
USGS Science Data Lifecycle Model uses Plan, Acquire, Process, Analyze, Preserve, and Publish/Share, plus cross-cuts: Describe, Manage Quality, Backup & Secure.
Harvard’s privacy-oriented guide stresses Plan → Create/Collect → Store → Use → Share → Archive/Destroy with security and minimization baked in.
Names differ; intent is shared: plan before you collect, document as you go, share responsibly, and retire data on purpose.

quiz.q: Which set matches NIST RDaF’s six high-level stages?
choices: Ingest, Transform, Load, Report, Alert, Patch
Envision, Plan, Generate/Acquire, Process/Analyze, Share/Use/Reuse, Preserve/Discard
quiz.explain: NIST RDaF Version 2.0 documents those six research-data lifecycle stages as its organizing structure.

sources.title: Introduction to the Data Lifecycle – UW–Madison
The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: A Learner-Friendly 7-Stage Model
modules.summary: Data Lens uses one simple spine for teaching: Plan → Create/Acquire → Store/Manage → Use/Process → Share → Archive → Destroy, with quality, security, and metadata as cross-cuts.
keyPoints: Plan: decide purpose, roles, classification, retention, and success measures before data arrives.
Create/Acquire: generate or collect data with consent, agreements, and capture standards in mind.
Store/Manage: place data in appropriate systems with backups, access control, and operational care.
Use/Process: transform, analyze, and interpret while preserving traceability of changes.
Share: publish or grant access under clear rules, licenses, and need-to-know limits.
Archive: keep what must persist for legal, scientific, or business value in durable form.
Destroy: securely delete what is no longer needed according to retention schedules.
Cross-cuts run through all stages: data quality, security/privacy, and metadata/lineage.

quiz.q: In the Data Lens 7-stage model, which activities are treated as cross-cuts?
quiz.explain: Cross-cuts are ongoing disciplines that apply at every stage rather than single destination steps.

modules.title: Stage: Plan
modules.summary: Planning is where you set purpose, roles, classification, formats, storage choices, sharing rules, and end-of-life expectations before collection begins.
keyPoints: Write a short data management plan: what you will collect, why, who decides, and how long you keep it.
Name a data owner (or equivalent decision-maker) early.
Classify sensitivity and minimize collection to what the purpose requires.
Anticipate sharing, reuse, and repository choices so formats stay usable.
Align with retention schedules and any contractual data-use terms.

quiz.q: Why define a data owner during planning?
choices: So nobody else can open a spreadsheet
To clarify who is accountable for decisions about access, retention, and stewardship
Because owners write all SQL by hand
quiz.explain: Ownership is about decision accountability, not typing every row.

sources.title: The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security
Introduction to the Data Lifecycle – UW–Madison

modules.title: Stage: Create / Acquire
modules.summary: Creation and acquisition are where raw data enters the organization—through sensors, forms, purchases, partners, or computation.
keyPoints: Prefer approved, secure transfer paths (encryption in transit where appropriate).
Honor data-use agreements and transparency expectations when collecting personal data.
Capture essential context at the source: units, timestamps, codes, and collection method.
Apply templates and standards so later integration is not a scavenger hunt.
Avoid creating unnecessary copies you forget to protect or delete.

quiz.q: A practical create/acquire habit is to:
choices: Collect every field ‘just in case’ forever
Capture purpose-needed data with enough context and agreement terms to use it safely later
Skip encryption because files are small
quiz.explain: Minimization plus documented context and agreements reduces risk and rework.

sources.title: The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: Stage: Store / Manage
modules.summary: Storage is not just disk space. It is ongoing care: location choice, encryption at rest, backups, access control, and operational monitoring.
keyPoints: Store data only in locations approved for its classification level.
Encrypt sensitive data at rest when policy requires it and keep keys managed.
Back up intentionally and test restores; backups are part of lifecycle, not optional extras.
Delete throwaway working copies after import or transformation.
IT custodians often implement these controls while owners and stewards set requirements.

quiz.q: Which store/manage practice reduces lingering risk after a transfer?
choices: Removing unnecessary working copies once the authoritative store is updated
Emailing production databases as attachments weekly
quiz.explain: Extra copies expand the attack and compliance surface; clean up when done.

sources.title: The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: Stage: Use / Process
modules.summary: Use and process cover cleaning, transforming, analyzing, modeling, and interpreting data to create insight—while keeping the trail understandable.
keyPoints: Document transformations so others can reproduce or audit results.
Use platforms with controls matching the data’s sensitivity.
Limit processing to stated purposes, especially for personal data.
Prefer reproducible workflows and versioned pipelines over one-off desktop magic.
Quality checks during processing catch issues before they become trusted metrics.

quiz.q: Why document processing steps?
choices: So future users can understand lineage, reproduce work, and trust results
quiz.explain: Traceable processing builds trust and supports reuse and audits.

sources.title: Introduction to the Data Lifecycle – UW–Madison
The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: Stage: Share
modules.summary: Sharing ranges from giving a teammate access to publishing open research data. Good sharing is intentional: right people, right terms, right protections.
keyPoints: Authenticate individuals; avoid shared passwords and uncontrolled public links for sensitive data.
Grant least privilege and revoke access when need ends.
For research or open data, use clear licenses, DOIs or persistent IDs where appropriate, and good metadata.
Curation (selection, documentation, packaging) makes reuse safer and more valuable.
Sensitive data may require repositories with controlled access rather than full open release.

quiz.q: A least-privilege sharing practice is to:
choices: Make every collaborator a full admin
Give named people only the access their role requires, then revoke when finished
quiz.explain: Named, limited, time-bounded access is a core sharing control.

sources.title: The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security
FAIR Guiding Principles – GO FAIR Foundation

modules.title: Stages: Archive and Destroy
modules.summary: End-of-life is a decision, not an accident. Archive what must persist; destroy what must not linger. Both need procedures and evidence.
keyPoints: Follow retention schedules and contractual timelines—keep no longer than necessary for the purpose.
Archiving means durable storage, readable formats, and metadata so future people can find and interpret the data.
Destruction means secure deletion across primary stores, copies, and relevant backups per policy.
Preserve/Discard in NIST RDaF and Archive/Destroy in privacy guides cover the same end-of-use idea.
Record what was archived or destroyed, by whom, and under which rule set.

quiz.q: Archive vs destroy—what is the key difference?
choices: Archive always means public GitHub; destroy means reboot
Archive keeps selected data for long-term value/compliance; destroy securely removes data that should no longer exist
quiz.explain: Both are deliberate end-of-use choices with different outcomes and controls.

sources.title: The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: What Data Governance Is (and Is Not)
modules.summary: Data governance is how an organization decides and oversees rules for data—who decides, what standards apply, and how accountability works. It is not a single tool or a legal department synonym.
keyPoints: Governance sets decision rights, policies, and escalation paths for data as an asset.
It enables consistent definitions, safer access, and clearer ownership across teams.
Governance is not the same as day-to-day data engineering, though it directs those practices.
In DAMA-DMBOK framing, governance sits at the center of related knowledge areas.
This track is educational overview—not legal advice for any jurisdiction.

quiz.q: Data governance primarily answers which question?
choices: Which GPU to buy this quarter?
Who decides what about data, under which policies, with what accountability?
quiz.explain: Governance focuses on decision rights, policies, and accountability.

modules.title: Decision Rights and Accountability
modules.summary: Clear decision rights prevent endless debates. Map which roles approve access, definitions, quality thresholds, retention, and exceptions.
keyPoints: Separate accountability (owns the outcome) from responsibility (does the work).
Domain owners typically approve policy for their data subjects; stewards operationalize standards.
Cross-domain conflicts escalate to a governance council or similar body.
Document decisions so newcomers inherit rules instead of tribal knowledge.
RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is a practical way to assign rights.

quiz.q: In a healthy RACI for a data domain, how many Accountable parties should there typically be?
choices: One clear Accountable owner for the outcome
quiz.explain: One Accountable party avoids diffusion of ownership.

sources.title: Data Owners vs Data Stewards vs Data Custodians – DataSunrise

modules.title: Policies, Standards, and Procedures
modules.summary: Policies state intent and constraints; standards make them measurable; procedures show how teams comply day to day.
keyPoints: Start with a short policy set: classification, access, quality expectations, retention, and acceptable use.
Standards define formats, naming, master entities, and metadata required fields.
Procedures and runbooks translate policy into tickets, reviews, and tool settings.
Keep policies living documents reviewed on a cadence; stale policy is ignored policy.
High-level privacy principles (e.g., purpose limitation, minimization) often shape enterprise policy language—always confirm with counsel for your jurisdiction.

quiz.q: Which pairing is most accurate?
choices: Policy = SQL query; Standard = keyboard shortcut
Policy = intent/rules; Standard = measurable conventions; Procedure = how to comply
quiz.explain: Layering policy → standard → procedure makes governance actionable.

sources.title: Art. 5 GDPR – Principles relating to processing of personal data
The Data Lifecycle – Harvard University Information Security

modules.title: Councils, Operating Models, and Sponsorship
modules.summary: Governance needs a forum and an operating rhythm: who meets, what they decide, and how work gets funded.
keyPoints: A data governance council (or equivalent) resolves cross-team standards and priority conflicts.
Executive sponsorship funds the program and removes blockers.
Operating models vary: federated stewards with a small center of excellence is common.
Measure adoption with concrete artifacts: approved glossary terms, access reviews completed, quality SLAs met.
Start narrow (critical domains) rather than boiling the ocean across all 11 knowledge areas at once.

quiz.q: A governance council is most useful for:
choices: Approving enterprise-wide standards and resolving cross-domain conflicts
quiz.explain: Councils provide cross-functional decision authority.

sources.title: DCAM Framework – EDM Council / EDM Association

modules.title: Metrics, Value, and Maturity Signals
modules.summary: Governance earns trust when it shows outcomes: fewer incidents, faster trusted analytics, clearer ownership—not vanity slide counts.
keyPoints: Track leading indicators (definitions published, owners assigned) and lagging ones (incident rates, audit findings).
Link metrics to business outcomes: reduced reconciliation time, improved customer contactability, cleaner regulatory reports.
Maturity models (e.g., DCAM for capability assessment; CMMI-style levels in some programs) help sequence improvement.
Avoid metric theater: if a KPI never changes decisions, drop or redesign it.
Reassess maturity periodically; governance is continuous improvement, not a one-time project.

quiz.q: DCAM is best described at a high level as:
choices: A capability assessment model for data management practices used to find gaps and plan improvements
quiz.explain: DCAM helps organizations assess and mature data management capabilities.

sources.title: DCAM Framework – EDM Council / EDM Association

modules.title: Risk, Compliance, and Related Frameworks (High-Level)
modules.summary: Governance intersects risk and compliance. Learn the landscape at a high level: privacy principles, IT governance frameworks, and security overlays—then involve specialists for binding advice.
keyPoints: GDPR Article 5 highlights principles such as lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.
COBIT focuses on enterprise governance and management of information and technology; it can sit alongside data-specific frameworks.
NIST privacy/cybersecurity frameworks often inform control libraries that data programs must respect.
Data Lens content is educational and not legal advice; implementers should consult qualified counsel and security teams.
Map regulations to concrete controls: classification, access reviews, retention jobs, and breach response playbooks.

quiz.q: Which is one of the GDPR Article 5 principles (high-level)?
choices: Always sell personal data by default
Data minimization—adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary
quiz.explain: Minimization is a core Article 5 principle; this module is educational, not legal advice.

quiz.q: COBIT is primarily associated with:
choices: Enterprise governance/management of information and technology
quiz.explain: ISACA’s COBIT is a widely used EGIT framework that can complement data management frameworks.

sources.title: Art. 5 GDPR – Principles relating to processing of personal data

modules.title: Data Governance
modules.summary: Data governance is the hub that sets policies, decision rights, and oversight so other data disciplines stay aligned and accountable.
keyPoints: Defines who may decide what about data domains, quality bars, and access.
Operates through councils, stewards, and documented escalation paths.
Connects business priorities to standards used by architecture, quality, and security teams.
Produces policies, RACI charts, issue logs, and compliance evidence.
Without governance, other knowledge areas drift into conflicting local rules.

quiz.q: In the classic DAMA Wheel visualization, where does Data Governance sit?
choices: At the center, coordinating other knowledge areas
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Architecture
modules.summary: Data architecture designs the target structures, platforms, and flow patterns so data supports strategy instead of accidental sprawl.
keyPoints: Creates blueprints for how domains, systems, and platforms relate.
Aligns technology choices with business capabilities and constraints.
Guides integration patterns, lake/warehouse strategies, and interface standards.
Works with enterprise architecture so data is not an afterthought.
Success looks like intentional landscapes rather than shadow IT sprawl.

quiz.q: Data architecture’s main job is to:
choices: Provide an intentional blueprint for data structures and flows aligned to enterprise goals
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Modeling & Design
modules.summary: Modeling turns business meaning into shared structures—conceptual, logical, and physical—so systems speak a common language.
keyPoints: Conceptual models capture business entities and relationships without storage details.
Logical models refine attributes, keys, and rules independent of a specific product.
Physical models implement storage for performance, integrity, and platform features.
Good models reduce ambiguity that later becomes quality incidents.
Design includes testing and maintenance as requirements change.

quiz.q: Which modeling level is most business-facing and storage-agnostic?
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Storage & Operations
modules.summary: Storage and operations keep structured data assets reliable: deploy, tune, back up, recover, and retire databases and filesystems responsibly.
keyPoints: Covers capacity, performance, availability, and operational procedures.
Includes backup/restore testing and environment management.
Implements retention and archival mechanics decided by governance.
Works closely with security for encryption, patching, and access layers.
Poor operations turn perfect models into outages and silent data loss.

quiz.q: A healthy storage & operations practice includes:
choices: Monitoring, backups with restore tests, and lifecycle retirement of obsolete stores
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Security
modules.summary: Data security protects confidentiality, integrity, and appropriate availability—especially for personal and regulated information—through controls and monitoring.
keyPoints: Classifies data and applies proportionate controls.
Uses access management, encryption, masking, and monitoring.
Supports privacy obligations and breach readiness in partnership with security teams.
Balances protection with legitimate business access needs.
Security requirements should be designed in, not bolted on after an incident.

quiz.q: Data security is best described as:
choices: Ensuring appropriate protection and access for data assets, including sensitive personal data
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Integration & Interoperability
modules.summary: Integration moves and aligns data across systems—batch, streaming, APIs, federation—so consumers get consistent, timely inputs.
keyPoints: Includes ETL/ELT, replication, APIs, and virtualization patterns.
Enforces contracts: schemas, SLAs, and error handling between producers and consumers.
Interoperability means systems can exchange and use data without endless one-off fixes.
Lineage from pipelines is essential metadata for trust.
Fragile point-to-point spaghetti is a common failure mode this discipline prevents.

quiz.q: Interoperability primarily means:
choices: Systems can exchange and make use of data through agreed formats and interfaces
Two teams share a coffee machine
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Documents & Content Management
modules.summary: Much organizational knowledge lives in documents, media, and other unstructured content. This area governs how that content is stored, classified, retained, and found.
keyPoints: Applies retention, access, and classification to files and content platforms.
Uses taxonomies, search, and records practices so content is findable.
Bridges unstructured content with structured data when analytics need both.
Reduces shadow content sprawl on unmanaged drives.
Treats content as governed information, not disposable clutter.

quiz.q: Documents & content management focuses on:
choices: Governing unstructured information assets such as documents and media across their lifecycle
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Reference & Master Data
modules.summary: Shared reference lists and master entities (customer, product, location) need deliberate management so every system uses consistent values and identities.
keyPoints: Reference data provides controlled codes and classifications used to categorize other data.
Master data manages core business entities shared across processes.
Goals include reducing duplicates and conflicting definitions.
Stewardship and matching rules create trusted ‘golden’ views where appropriate.
Poor master/reference practice breaks reporting and customer experience.

quiz.q: Country codes used to classify addresses are typically:
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence
modules.summary: Warehousing and BI organize analytical data and deliver trustworthy reporting and self-service insight for decisions.
keyPoints: Structures curated analytical data for consumption (warehouses, marts, lakehouse patterns).
Depends on upstream quality, modeling, and integration discipline.
Includes semantic layers, certified metrics, and access controls for reports.
Separates exploratory sandboxes from certified production metrics when needed.
BI value collapses if definitions of ‘revenue’ differ by dashboard.

quiz.q: A common failure mode for BI programs is:
choices: Too much agreement on metric definitions
Conflicting metric definitions across dashboards due to weak upstream governance
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Metadata Management
modules.summary: Metadata is data about data: definitions, ownership, lineage, sensitivity tags, and technical descriptors that make assets understandable and governable.
keyPoints: Business metadata explains meaning; technical metadata describes structure and jobs; operational metadata covers run history.
Catalogs and glossaries help people find and trust assets.
Lineage shows where data came from and where it goes.
Metadata enables automation: classification, access, and quality rules.
Without metadata, every reuse starts with reverse-engineering.

quiz.q: Lineage metadata primarily helps you:
choices: Trace origins and downstream impacts of a dataset or field
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Data Quality Management
modules.summary: Data quality management defines what ‘fit for use’ means, measures it, and drives remediation so decisions rest on dependable data.
keyPoints: Common teaching dimensions include accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness.
Profile data, set rules/thresholds, monitor, and fix root causes—not only symptoms.
Quality is cross-functional: modeling, stewardship, and pipelines all contribute.
Prioritize critical data elements tied to real decisions or obligations.
Continuous improvement beats one-time cleansing projects.

quiz.q: Which set lists widely taught core data quality dimensions?
choices: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness
quiz.explain: This module summarizes the knowledge area in original learner language based on public DAMA-DMBOK overviews.

modules.title: Owner, Steward, and Custodian
modules.summary: Three complementary roles keep decision rights, caretaking, and technical controls from collapsing into one overloaded person.
keyPoints: Data Owner: senior accountability for a domain—approves policies, access principles, and quality expectations.
Data Steward: domain expert who maintains definitions, monitors quality, and translates policy into practice.
Data Custodian: typically IT/platform role that implements storage, security, backups, and access mechanics.
Owners decide ‘what/why’; stewards handle ‘how’ day-to-day; custodians run the systems.
Small organizations may combine roles, but should still separate accountability from pure administration.

quiz.q: Who typically configures database permissions after an access decision?
choices: Only the CEO personally every time
Often the data custodian implementing owner/steward-approved rules
quiz.explain: Custodians implement technical controls; they do not usually set business policy alone.

sources.title: Data Owners vs Data Stewards vs Data Custodians – DataSunrise
Your role: Data Steward – ELIXIR RDMkit

modules.title: Councils, CDO, and Executive Sponsors
modules.summary: Enterprise programs need visible leadership: a chief data officer (or equivalent), sponsors, and a council that can make cross-team calls stick.
keyPoints: Executive sponsors secure budget and prioritize governance work against competing projects.
A CDO or data lead coordinates strategy across domains and platforms.
Councils approve shared standards and mediate conflicts between domains.
Working groups handle deep dives (glossary, quality rules) and bring proposals upward.
Authority without expertise fails; expertise without authority stalls—balance both.

quiz.q: Why does a governance program need executive sponsorship?
choices: To fund work, remove blockers, and signal that data decisions are organizational priorities
quiz.explain: Sponsorship provides air cover and resources for sustained change.

modules.title: Using RACI for Data Decisions
modules.summary: RACI clarifies who does the work, who owns the outcome, who must be consulted, and who is informed—especially for access, quality, and retention.
keyPoints: Responsible people perform the activity; Accountable people own the result (one preferred).
Consulted stakeholders give input before decisions; Informed parties hear outcomes after.
Apply RACI to recurring governance activities: classification, access reviews, MDM changes, retention exceptions.
Publish the matrix where teams look for process, not only in a forgotten slide deck.
Revisit RACI when org structures or platforms change.

quiz.q: In RACI, ‘C’ usually means:
quiz.explain: Consulted parties contribute expertise before a decision is finalized.

sources.title: Data Owners vs Data Stewards vs Data Custodians – DataSunrise

modules.title: FAIR Thinking and Stewardship Culture
modules.summary: FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) give stewards a shared north star for making data usable by humans and machines—complementing, not replacing, ethics and CARE-style community considerations where relevant.
keyPoints: Findable: persistent identifiers and rich, indexed metadata.
Accessible: retrieval via standard protocols with auth where needed; metadata may remain available even if data cannot.
Interoperable: shared vocabularies and qualified references between datasets.
Reusable: clear licenses, provenance, and community standards.
Stewardship culture rewards documentation and quality as first-class work, not unpaid overtime.

quiz.q: FAIR’s ‘F’ stands for:
quiz.explain: Findability is the first FAIR pillar.

sources.title: FAIR Guiding Principles – GO FAIR Foundation
Your role: Data Steward – ELIXIR RDMkit

modules.title: Data Quality Dimensions
modules.summary: Quality dimensions are lenses for measuring fitness for use. Six dimensions appear again and again in practitioner teaching.
keyPoints: Accuracy: values correctly represent the real-world or trusted source.
Completeness: required fields and records are present.
Consistency: the same fact agrees across systems or records.
Timeliness: data is available and current when decisions need it.
Validity: values obey formats, ranges, and business rules.
Uniqueness: entities are not unintentionally duplicated.
Organizations may add integrity, precision, or relevance to fit their context.

quiz.q: A birth date recorded as a future date most clearly fails which dimension?
quiz.explain: Rule-breaking values are validity failures; they may also be inaccurate.

sources.title: What Are Data Quality Dimensions? – IBM

modules.title: Measuring, Monitoring, and Improving Quality
modules.summary: Dimensions become useful when turned into rules, thresholds, dashboards, and root-cause fixes.
keyPoints: Profile data to discover nulls, outliers, and duplicates before setting targets.
Define critical data elements and SLAs with business owners.
Automate checks in pipelines; alert stewards when thresholds breach.
Prefer fixing upstream processes over endless downstream cleansing.
Report trends to the governance forum so quality stays funded.

quiz.q: After detecting recurring incomplete addresses, the best long-term move is usually to:
choices: Fix the capture process upstream and monitor completeness
quiz.explain: Sustainable quality comes from preventing defects at the source.

sources.title: What Are Data Quality Dimensions? – IBM

modules.title: Types of Metadata
modules.summary: Different metadata types answer different questions: what does it mean, how is it stored, how did it run, and who may see it?
keyPoints: Business metadata: definitions, owners, glossary terms, certified metrics.
Technical metadata: schemas, column types, jobs, and physical locations.
Operational metadata: freshness, run success/failure, volumes, SLAs.
Governance metadata: classification, retention tags, access policies.
A catalog that only lists tables without meaning still leaves users guessing.

quiz.q: A glossary definition of ‘active customer’ is primarily:
quiz.explain: Business metadata captures shared meaning for people and processes.

modules.title: Lineage, Catalogs, and Discovery
modules.summary: Catalogs help people find assets; lineage explains impact and provenance—together they underpin trust and safe change.
keyPoints: Data catalogs inventory assets with searchable metadata and ownership.
Lineage traces fields and datasets from sources through transforms to reports.
Impact analysis uses lineage before changing a critical upstream field.
Discovery without access governance creates risk; pair findability with controls.
FAIR findability depends on rich metadata registered in searchable resources.

quiz.q: Before renaming a widely used customer ID field, teams should check:
choices: Lineage/impact to see which pipelines and reports depend on it
quiz.explain: Lineage prevents surprise breakages across the estate.

sources.title: FAIR Guiding Principles – GO FAIR Foundation

modules.title: Applying FAIR in Practice
modules.summary: FAIR is a set of guiding principles, not a certificate sticker. Apply them proportionally to research and enterprise sharing goals.
keyPoints: Assign persistent identifiers and keep metadata linked to those IDs.
Publish enough metadata for humans and machines to evaluate reuse.
Use open, standard protocols for access; add auth when data cannot be fully open.
Adopt community vocabularies and clear usage licenses.
Document provenance so others know how the data was produced.

quiz.q: Which practice supports FAIR Reusability?
choices: Hide the license and erase provenance
Provide a clear usage license plus rich provenance and community-relevant standards
Use only private slang with no documentation
quiz.explain: Reusable data needs licenses, provenance, and standards-aligned description.

sources.title: FAIR Guiding Principles – GO FAIR Foundation

modules.title: What Is Master Data?
modules.summary: Master data describes the core business entities an organization repeatedly relies on—customers, products, suppliers, locations—and needs a trusted shared view.
keyPoints: Master data is typically more stable and widely reused than raw transactions.
Without MDM, each system invents its own conflicting customer or product records.
Creating a ‘golden record’ involves matching, merging, and stewarding conflicting sources.
Domains often include customer, product, supplier, and location (plus industry-specific entities).
MDM is as much process and stewardship as it is software.

quiz.q: A reconciled single customer profile used across CRM and billing is an example of:
choices: A temporary cache with no owner
quiz.explain: MDM aims for consistent core entity data across systems.

sources.title: What is Master Data Management? – IBM

modules.title: What Is Reference Data?
modules.summary: Reference data is the controlled vocabulary used to classify and validate other data—codes, lists, and standard values.
keyPoints: Examples: country codes, currency codes, status lists, product category taxonomies.
Good reference data improves validity and consistency for transactional and master records.
Reference lists need owners, versioning, and change control when values evolve.
Reference data is usually simpler than master entities but still mission-critical.
Conflicting code lists across systems create silent reporting errors.

quiz.q: ISO country codes used in address forms are best classified as:
quiz.explain: Codes that classify other data are classic reference data.

sources.title: What is Master Data Management? – IBM

modules.title: MDM vs Reference Data Management
modules.summary: MDM and reference data management (RDM) are related but not identical. Know when you need entity resolution versus controlled lists.
keyPoints: RDM governs code sets and classifications; MDM governs shared business entities and relationships.
MDM often consumes reference data (e.g., valid country codes on a customer record).
MDM challenges include matching, survivorship rules, and hierarchy management.
RDM challenges include versioning lists, effective dating, and distributing updates.
Both need stewardship, quality rules, and clear ownership—just at different scopes.

quiz.q: Which statement is most accurate?
choices: MDM and RDM are always the exact same discipline with identical scope
RDM manages controlled lists/codes; MDM manages core shared entities—often used together
quiz.explain: They complement each other: lists vs entities.

quiz.q: Survivorship rules are most associated with:
choices: Choosing which source values win when building a master golden record
quiz.explain: Survivorship decides winning attribute values during master merge.
